name: Testagen

lead: Testagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly) is a short peptide in the Khavinson bioregulator family, promoted in research-peptide and longevity communities for testicular function and testosterone. Users link higher testosterone to muscle, leanness and masculine features.

The chain runs from testicular support to higher testosterone to a leaner, more muscular look. Published work shows that labelled short peptides including Testagen can enter cultured cells and nuclei, and a 2025 materials paper studied it as a copper-corrosion inhibitor. No studies in people were found.

paras: It is used in periodic courses in research-peptide routines, sometimes alongside other hormone-support approaches.
No human safety data were found. It is not an approved medicine and is sold unregulated as a research chemical.

angle.text: Testagen is promoted in research-peptide communities as supporting testicular function and testosterone, which users link to muscle, leanness and masculine features. The claim comes from developer material; no human studies have been published.

lead: Testagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly (KEDG), part of the family of short "bioregulator" peptides associated with Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia [1]. It is promoted in research-peptide and longevity communities as supporting testicular function and testosterone.

Evidence is very thin. A laboratory study showed that fluorescent-labeled short peptides including Testagen can enter cells and nuclei in culture [1], and a 2025 materials-science paper examined Testagen as a copper-corrosion inhibitor [2]. No studies of Testagen in people were found.

paras: Fluorescein-labeled Testagen, along with epithalon and pinealon, was seen in the cytoplasm, nucleus and nucleolus of HeLa cells, and the authors reported in vitro interactions of such peptides with DNA oligonucleotides [1]. This work does not address effects on the testes or hormones. A 2025 paper studied the peptide's adsorption on copper surfaces in salt solution, an unrelated chemistry application [2].

No studies found. A registry entry titled "Testagen TDS-Testosterone" (NCT02733133) concerns a transdermal testosterone product with a similar brand name; it is registered as not yet recruiting and is not evidently about this peptide [3].

Testagen is sold as a research chemical and is not approved as a medicine. Claims about testosterone support come from vendor and community material; no published human data were found to evaluate them.
